video_title: The $25 Trillion AI Robotics Revolution: Are We Ready?
gist: Sue Enis, former Hut 8 head of IR and now president of Realbotics' direct-to-consumer arm (Intima AI / RealDoll), makes the case for AI companion robots and intimacy hardware as assistive tools for lonely, disabled and elderly users. She sizes AI-companion demand at 680M monthly users, describes a hardware-plus-subscription model and the Realbotics NASDAQ uplist/split, and recounts Hut 8's pivot from Bitcoin mining to AI power. The '$25 trillion' figure in the title is never discussed in the transcript.

insights.claim: Realbotics is splitting into two separate companies with separate management teams and P&Ls: Realbotics (healthcare/education humanoid robotics) is uplisting to the NASDAQ, while Intima AI (owner of RealDoll, direct-to-consumer intimacy hardware) stays on the TSXV with Sue Enis as CEO and may eventually uplist to NASDAQ.
insights.speaker: Sue Enis
insights.so_what: Corporate separation and NASDAQ uplisting are catalysts that can change liquidity and investor base for both entities; watch the spin/uplist timing.

insights.claim: RealDoll has handmade intimacy hardware in the USA since 1996 from a warehouse about 10 minutes off the Las Vegas Strip, has served over 50,000 customers, and claims ~120,000 newsletter subscribers, 65,000 Instagram followers and a fan forum with ~110,000 active users.
insights.speaker: Sue Enis
insights.so_what: Gives a sense of the installed base and brand reach a small-cap intimacy-hardware business is building its AI subscription on.

insights.claim: Realbotics' healthcare pitch is human-looking robots that sit with cognitively impaired elderly patients, remind them about medication and walks, and feed interaction data back to family and healthcare providers, positioned as a response to a shortage of elder-care providers.
insights.speaker: Sue Enis
insights.so_what: Frames humanoid companion robots as an elder-care labor-shortage play rather than a consumer novelty; watch for healthcare pilots or contracts.

insights.claim: Sue Enis argues that elderly and cognitively impaired people are not evolutionarily wired to connect with screens, so a realistic embodied robot is a better interface for them than a tablet or app, and cites a UK study where elderly users of assistive AI companions gained confidence from mastering the technology.
insights.speaker: Sue Enis
insights.so_what: Supports the thesis that embodiment (hardware) rather than chat apps captures value in elder-care AI.
insights.quote: we are not wired from an evolutionary perspective to actually connect with the screen

insights.claim: Sue Enis cites roughly 680 million people globally and 35 million in the US using AI companion chat apps monthly, with multiple reports saying 28% of those 35 million US users have had an intimate experience with a chatbot.
insights.speaker: Sue Enis
insights.so_what: Sizes the addressable base of users who might pay to 'embody' an existing screen relationship in hardware.
insights.quote: there's something like 680 million people globally who use AI companion, just the chat apps monthly

insights.claim: Sue Enis believes the spread of ChatGPT, Replika and Character.ai has pushed AI intimacy to a tipping point where it is going mainstream.
insights.speaker: Sue Enis
insights.so_what: Mainstreaming of AI companionship expands demand for adjacent hardware, middleware and subscription businesses.
insights.quote: this is kind of like the tipping point of this going even more mainstream on the intimacy side

insights.claim: RealDoll's customer base is roughly 50/50 men and women and includes disabled people, veterans with PTSD, neurodivergent people, isolated people in remote areas, lonely divorcees and empty-nesters, and married couples seeking novelty.
insights.speaker: Sue Enis
insights.so_what: Challenges the stereotype of a narrow male customer base; the gender split points to underserved demand for female- and LGBTQ-oriented products.

insights.claim: Sue Enis attributes the loneliness epidemic to convenience culture and engagement-maximizing platforms (food delivery, DMs, infinite scroll), citing that about 5% of South Korea's population goes 30+ days without speaking to anyone.
insights.speaker: Sue Enis
insights.so_what: Social isolation is a secular demand driver for companion technology across consumer and healthcare channels.

insights.claim: Sue Enis says the intimacy-hardware market has been shaped by a single heterosexual-male perspective, leaving male dolls, products for women and LGBTQ customers underserved; she reports huge demand for male companions and around 10 emails a day asking for a Henry Cavill likeness.
insights.speaker: Sue Enis
insights.so_what: Signals a product-gap growth vector (male companions, female/LGBTQ buyers) that incumbents may be missing.

insights.claim: RealDoll created North America's first AI companion robot, Harmony, in 2018, built on GPT-2 with memory of prior conversations; 12 robots of the latest AI iteration are now with beta testers, with heads having about 24 degrees of freedom so they blink, talk and remember users, but they cannot walk.
insights.speaker: Sue Enis
insights.so_what: Shows the product is a stationary embodied companion, not a bipedal humanoid; roadmap explicitly excludes walking 'robot partners'.

insights.claim: Intima AI's business model is hardware sales (lifelike dolls plus handheld devices) bundled with an AI character subscription, plus a middleware layer that lets users import a relationship built with a screen-based AI into its hardware; the subscription is expected to be ready to scale by the end of December.
insights.speaker: Sue Enis
insights.so_what: Recurring subscription revenue on top of premium hardware is the key model shift to watch; the year-end launch is a near-term milestone.

insights.claim: Intima AI positions itself as a premium, US-made provider that will not compete with cheap Chinese products, citing trusted materials and legal recourse; it might outsource some physical production to China at scale but would keep the technology American.
insights.speaker: Sue Enis
insights.so_what: Premium pricing plus US manufacturing implies higher margins but scaling constraints; payment plans are being added to address the high price point.
insights.quote: we're not trying to compete with cheap Chinese products

insights.claim: Intima AI deliberately builds friction into its AI companions instead of 24/7 engagement and mirroring; one persona, Maya, was given so much friction that customers complained she was rude and she had to be softened.
insights.speaker: Sue Enis
insights.so_what: Contrasts with engagement-maximizing chatbot designs that are drawing lawsuits; a design choice that may reduce regulatory risk but also engagement.

insights.claim: Intima AI says it stores no customer interaction data in the cloud and does not listen to conversations; all personal interaction data stays on the user's device.
insights.speaker: Sue Enis
insights.so_what: Privacy-first architecture is a differentiator for a discretion-sensitive category and lowers data-liability risk.

insights.claim: Sue Enis argues AI regulation should mirror crypto's path to rules like the CLARITY Act: government guidelines co-written with builders so people can innovate safely, rather than either shutting AI down or leaving it to a duopoly of leaders like Dario Amodei and Elon Musk.
insights.speaker: Sue Enis
insights.so_what: Favors a regulatory outcome that preserves open-source and smaller players; heavy-handed or incumbent-captured regulation would hurt companies like hers.
insights.quote: creating a duopoly and a monopoly can also go horribly wrong

insights.claim: Sue Enis warns that regulating AI out of existence in the US, as Bernie Sanders proposes, would not stop China or Russia from innovating and would leave the US behind.
insights.speaker: Sue Enis
insights.so_what: Geopolitical competition is the main argument against restrictive US AI policy; watch policy rhetoric for risk to US AI builders.

insights.claim: Sue Enis calls for more transparency from AI labs, saying a whistleblower warning from Anthropic about AI danger should come with specifics about what in the code or frameworks caused concern.
insights.speaker: Sue Enis
insights.so_what: Signals pressure for AI-lab disclosure standards as safety narratives shape regulation.

themes.theme: Hut 8: miners pivot to AI power

insights.claim: Around summer 2024, hyperscalers and AI infrastructure operators realized the US lacked enough power and had antiquated grids, which made Bitcoin miners sitting on large power capacity a potential solution for AI compute.
insights.speaker: Sue Enis
insights.so_what: Core reason Bitcoin miners re-rated as AI-power plays; power access is the scarce asset.
insights.quote: Bitcoin miners, we were all sitting on a ton of power

insights.claim: Hut 8 spun its Bitcoin mining machines into American Bitcoin, a partnership with the Trumps in which Hut 8 last owned about 60%, while the Hut 8 parent focuses solely on energy infrastructure and has signed a deal with Anthropic as a customer.
insights.speaker: Sue Enis
insights.so_what: Hut 8 is now an energy/AI-infrastructure company with a large stake in a pure-play miner; Anthropic as customer is a credibility marker.

insights.claim: Hut 8 traded at 40 cents when Sue Enis joined as head of IR in December 2020 and had become a mid-cap with Anthropic as a customer, a world-class board and Coatue (captioned 'Code 2') as an investor by December 2025; she left on March 16, 2026 and remains a Hut 8 holder, backing CEO Asher Genoot.
insights.speaker: Sue Enis
insights.so_what: A former insider still holding and endorsing management is a soft positive signal for Hut 8.

insights.claim: Sue Enis's framework: the team that takes a company from $10 million to $1 billion differs from the team that takes it from $3 billion to $10 billion or $100 billion, so early-stage operators should exit as a company institutionalizes.
insights.speaker: Sue Enis
insights.so_what: Useful lens for judging management transitions as small caps become institutional.
insights.quote: the people who take you from like 10 million to a billion are much different than the people who take you from like 3 billion to 10 billion

insights.claim: Sue Enis says AI and intimacy today look like crypto in 2016: hundreds of millions of dollars flying around, nascent technology, no rules and few diverse perspectives, which is why she moved from Hut 8 into the sector.
insights.speaker: Sue Enis
insights.so_what: Positions AI companionship as an early, misunderstood, unregulated category, where she expects a crypto-like path toward rules and wider acceptance over 5-10 years.
insights.quote: A lot of what I started to see in AI looked a lot like what I saw in crypto in 2016.

insights.claim: Intima AI is exploring letting users opt in to share their companion interaction data privately and be paid in crypto for it, using crypto rails, on the view that data is the new oil for AI training.
insights.speaker: Sue Enis
insights.so_what: An early signal of user-paid data marketplaces for AI training, where crypto rails could handle payments and privacy.

insights.claim: Intima AI has discussed accepting Bitcoin for discreet purchases, and Sue Enis expects agent-to-agent micropayments over privacy-preserving crypto rails to play a role.
insights.speaker: Sue Enis
insights.so_what: A small, speculative use case for Bitcoin and stablecoin payments in AI commerce; not yet on a firm roadmap.
